title: Metric Harmonization & Load Protocols - Lyra Systems Benchmark Workshop
next_steps: Send apples-to-apples protocol draft and CSV of prompt groups
Share small-sample load script and runbook for on-prem agent
Schedule 2-hour lab session to run baseline traces (week of 2026-02-24)
action_items: Janelle Park - Draft metric harmonization doc and baseline prompt taxonomy (due 2026-02-21)
Marcus Chen - Share synthetic load generator and example config for KV-cache warmup (due 2026-02-18)
Owen McBride - Provision VPN/VPC connectivity test and confirm network egress path (due 2026-02-19)
summary: Deep technical workshop to align on apples-to-apples benchmarking methodology for runtime and latency throughput comparisons across hosted, dedicated, and on-prem variants. Emphasis on metric harmonization (p95/p99, tail latency vs P50), KV cache warmup protocols, batching profiles, quantization impact, and reproducible load generation. Agreed next steps: Redwood to deliver protocol draft and scripts; Lyra to provision connectivity and a small pilot dataset for prompt-run validation.
transcript:
[00:00] Janelle Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we got about an hour and a bit, maybe 75, 80 minutes. quick intro round?
[00:18] Samira Qureshi: Hi, Samira from Lyra, CTO. excited, been looking forward to aligning on how we run apples-to-apples.
[00:28] Priya Nair: Priya here, head of ML, mostly focused on latency budgets and model quality drift.
[00:36] Marcus Chen: Marcus from Redwood eng - I'll drive the bench configs and load scripts.
[00:45] Owen McBride: Owen SRE, I'll handle network and infra questions.
[00:51] Jordan Li: Jordan, ML eng, will run prompt curation and local sampling.
[00:56] Janelle Park: Cool. goal for today is to harmonize metrics and agree a repeatable protocol for comparing hosted vs dedicated vs Lyra's on-prem test cluster. also decide on prompt sets and how we do KV-cache warmup.
[01:12] Priya Nair: Quick note - our primary KPI is p95 < 200ms for user-facing completions at 1.2k qps, but we also care about cost per 1M tokens. so both latency and unit cost need to be comparable.
[01:34] Marcus Chen: Right, so first callout: apples-to-apples means same model binary, same tokenizer, same sequence lengths, and identical batching logic where possible. for quantized variants we should define the quant level in the protocol (e.g., int8/4-bit) and document exact toolchain for quantization.
[01:58] Samira Qureshi: For on-prem we may not have the same CUDA driver version as Redwood hosted - how do we account for that?
[02:11] Marcus Chen: Good — document the hardware/driver matrix. our suggestion: record GPU model, driver, CUDA/cuDNN versions, and include kernel versions; then run kernel selection warmups. we'll include a small checklist in the protocol.
[02:28] [02:30] Jordan Li: (quiet) can we talk about prompt sets? we have a big mix: short queries, long multi-turn, and code completions.
[02:40] Janelle Park: Yes. we propose three canonical prompt groups: micro (<=32 tokens), standard (33-256), and long-context (257-1024). within each group we pick 50 representative prompts. that lets us measure latency distribution across length buckets.
[03:05] Priya Nair: Sounds reasonable. how do we ensure semantic parity? we don't want prompts that favor a caching win for hosted because of popular prefixes.
[03:14] Marcus Chen: That's where randomness and seed control come in. the protocol will specify a fixed shuffle seed, and for each run we'll rotate the prompt order and ensure identical prompt inputs across all environments. also keep a versioned prompt CSV.
[03:31] Owen McBride: about KV cache - Lyra will run on-prem with a local filesystem-backed cache. what's the warmup procedure?
[03:44] Marcus Chen: For KV-cache: two stages. cold-run then warm-run. cold-run starts with empty cache and measures first-window latencies; warm-run preloads prefix KV entries from a saved trace for N tokens or runs a deterministic warmup script that issues the first 500 unique prefixes at low QPS until TTLs are populated. the protocol will define warmup length by model context size (e.g., preload until KV store reaches ~80% of observed working set).
[04:14] Samira Qureshi: does warmup falsify cost comparisons? if we preload heavily, hosted might use shared caches differently.
[04:26] Janelle Park: We'll capture both cold and steady-state metrics. apples-to-apples: compare steady-state after identical warmup protocols, and report cold-start separately.
[04:40] [04:45] Jordan Li: batching strategy question — what batch sizes? ours currently batch aggressively to save cost but that adds 50-150ms tail depending on request mix.
[04:57] Marcus Chen: The plan: run at a set of target latency SLOs (e.g., P95 targets 100ms, 200ms, 400ms) and for each target measure the batching config that yields max throughput under that SLO. the protocol will include a table: target SLO -> allowed batching windows (ms) and max batch size. we'll also log effective tokens-per-second and cost per token.
[05:25] Priya Nair: and quantization? we want to understand quality delta for int8 and 4-bit QAT variants.
[05:33] Marcus Chen: We'll include a quality evaluation step: run the same prompt set against full fp16 baseline and quantized variant, compute ROUGE/BLEU for structured outputs or embedding cosine similarity for semantic tasks, and flag any dropout > X% by metric. also include human spot checks for hallucination.
[05:58] Samira Qureshi: Ok. on security - Lyra needs to verify network paths. our compliance team wants to see encryption in transit, KMS usage for keys, and audit logs for inference calls.
[06:12] Janelle Park: Redwood can run a private agent in Lyra's VPC for the pilot. we'll provide docs for our private control plane and an on-prem agent with HSM/KMS hooks. we'll share compliance docs and SOC artifacts as a follow-up.
[06:28] Owen McBride: For the on-prem agent, do you run the control plane in our VPC or do we pull from you? need to know about egress connections for telemetry.
[06:40] Marcus Chen: Options: 1) outbound-only control-plane to Redwood managed endpoints with mTLS, or 2) self-hosted control plane where you keep everything internal. for the pilot we'd likely use option 1 with explicit allow-listing. we'll document telemetry granularity and retention window.
[06:59] [07:05] Jordan Li: load generation — what's your recommended ramp pattern? linear ramp, step, or sawtooth?
[07:15] Marcus Chen: We suggest a three-phase pattern: ramp-up (linear to target over 2 minutes), steady-state (10-15 minutes at target QPS), then stress window (short bursts at 1.5-2x target for 3 minutes). repeat this for each conf. record CPU/GPU utilization, queue depths, and per-token latency histograms.
[07:42] Priya Nair: how do we compare throughput when the models use different quant kernels and different CUDA kernels?
[07:52] Marcus Chen: record kernel-level metrics and normalize throughput by tokens/sec and cost-per-token. don't compare raw GPU utilization alone. the protocol will include a normalization appendix: throughput-per-GPU-hour and tokens-per-dollar normalized to a standard price matrix (we'll provide our cost model for the hosted case, Lyra can substitute their internal cost numbers).
[08:18] [08:30] Samira Qureshi: competing products may do smarter caching or request collapsing. should we mention them in the report?
[08:38] Janelle Park: we'll note architectural differences in the appendix (e.g., request collapsing, prefix sharing). if you want head-to-head we can run a limited comparative test but that requires explicit configurations and is a different engagement.
[08:57] Marcus Chen: quick demo time — I have a sample load script and a minimal CSV of prompts. show the warmup sequence and how the metrics are captured.
[09:10] [09:16] Marcus Chen shares screen: gist.github.com/... (redacted link)
[09:22] Marcus Chen: here's the script; it supports k6 and a lightweight Python runner. important flags: --seed, --batch-window-ms, --warmup-requests, --concurrency.
[09:35] Jordan Li: I see a --kv-warmup-file option. how do we generate that?
[09:40] Marcus Chen: Use captured prefixes from a production trace or generate synthetic prefixes from your prompt set by truncating to context breakpoints. we'll include a helper script to create a KV warmup file from a prompt CSV.
[09:56] Priya Nair: can we run the baseline now on our dev cluster with a small sample?
[10:02] Owen McBride: we can, but we need VPN keys and a small memory allocation. I can provision a 4 GPU test box for the run.
[10:08] Janelle Park: Great — we'll coordinate offline.
[10:12] [10:15] Samira Qureshi: One thought: when you report p99, please annotate whether that p99 is measured at request completion or token emission — that changes the numbers for streaming workloads.
[10:28] Marcus Chen: Good point. protocol will define: p95/99 request-completion latencies and token-level emission latencies for streaming endpoints separately.
[10:36] Jordan Li: also include failure modes and retries; how the client should interpret 500 vs 429 vs 202 responses during stress.
[10:45] Marcus Chen: we'll log error rates and retry counts and include guidelines for backoff.
[10:52] [11:00] Priya Nair: I want to make sure cost numbers are comparable. Redwood hosted has volume discounts; Lyra's internal cost base is different. how do we normalize?
[11:10] Janelle Park: We'll produce two cost columns: raw provider cost (e.g., per-GPU-hour using a reference cloud price) and an adjusted cost-per-token using your internal cost inputs. that'll be a small table in the final report.
[11:30] [11:45] Owen McBride: Network latency and egress — for on-prem tests we'll capture RTT to Redwood endpoints and include network jitter in the appendix.
[11:55] Marcus Chen: Yes, capture both application-level RTT and lower-level metrics (tcptrace, etc). we'll provide the collection hooks.
[12:10] [12:30] Janelle Park: Let's walk through a sample run config. target QPS 1k across micro+standard mix, p95 target 200ms, warmup 10 minutes, repeat 3 cycles. what logs and traces do you need Lyra to share?
[12:46] Jordan Li: we'll share GPU metrics, top-level process metrics, and a single anonymized prompt CSV. no PII.
[12:58] Priya Nair: also add a note to the protocol about random seed reproducibility for tokenizers and any library-level nondeterminism.
[13:08] Marcus Chen: noted. we'll include library versions and a deterministic env file.
[13:18] [13:30] Samira Qureshi: timeline — we'd like initial baseline results in two weeks. realistic?
[13:38] Janelle Park: yes, if we get connectivity and the prompt CSV this week, we can run a baseline and share an initial report in ~10 business days.
[13:50] Marcus Chen: One more nuance: quantization vendor toolchains differ; any quantization step must be checked by model quality tests. we will include the exact quant command-lines.
[14:05] Jordan Li: ok. question about telemetry: are you sampling traces or keeping full flamegraphs? storage could be heavy.
[14:16] Marcus Chen: default is sampling plus full traces for stress windows. we'll parameterize sampling rate in the runbook.
[14:30] [14:45] Owen McBride: Security question again — what audit logs do you need? just request ids and hashes?
[14:56] Janelle Park: request-id, user-id hash, timestamp, route/model, and token counts. no raw prompt content unless explicitly allowed. for SOC/ISO we can provide redacted logs.
[15:14] [15:30] Samira Qureshi: can Redwood help with the run itself? an SE-assisted lab?
[15:39] Marcus Chen: yes, we'll offer a 2-hour assisted lab session to run the first baseline. that's one of the next steps.
[15:48] Janelle Park: Recap: Redwood sends protocol doc + scripts (Marcus), Lyra provisions VPN and provides prompt CSV and test box (Owen), Redwood runs assisted lab (Marcus + Janelle). deliverables timeline around 2026-02-21 for protocol and 2026-02-24 for the lab.
[16:09] [16:20] Priya Nair: sounds good. any objections?
[16:23] Samira Qureshi: none.
[16:26] Jordan Li: none.
[16:28] Marcus Chen: I'll also attach a small sample results CSV format so we all agree on columns: timestamp, request_id, prompt_group, input_tokens, output_tokens, latency_ms, status_code, gpu_util, batch_size, kv_hit_rate.
[16:49] Janelle Park: Perfect. we'll share that with the protocol. thanks everyone.
[16:55] [17:00] Samira Qureshi: Thanks. bye.
[17:02] Priya Nair: bye.
[17:05] Marcus Chen: bye.
[17:08] Owen McBride: end of recording.
